title: UX Job Security
intro: The amount of bad UX still shipping is the case for optimism.

learn.title: The heuristic review
learn.text:
A visually stunning site failed on basics the stakeholders accepted immediately:

• Four differently worded buttons (“Talk to a Representative”, “Compare Options”…) that all opened the same form
• A gallery that swapped one stock photo for another
• Hover-dependent multi-level navigation that collapsed if the pointer drifted
• Top-level items that opened menus on hover but navigated on click

Problems known for about **40 years**. The team simply agreed.

try.q: What does the review's outcome suggest about demand for UX expertise?
options: There is still plenty of basic work to do
Visual design is the main gap
try.explain: The problems were decades old and nobody had caught them.

learn.title: What the layoff data shows
learn.text:
Lawton Pybus's analysis of 12 layoff directories covering 5,521 people:

• Engineering — **27%**
• Product and Program — **11%**
• All UX roles — **8.7%**
• UX Design — **3.9%**
• UX Research — **2.3%**

**These are directory shares, not layoff probabilities.** UX may still be hit hard relative to its size — the data says UX isn't being cut first, not that it's safe.

options: Shares of people listed in layoff directories
The probability of being laid off
The share of currently open roles by discipline
try.explain: Share of a directory isn't risk, because it doesn't account for how many people hold each role.

left.label: The claim
items: Research is the most exposed role

right.label: The data
items: UX roles are 8.7% of those listed

learn.title: Expert in the loop
learn.text:
AI makes experts faster but **can't supply the expertise to tell good output from plausible output**.

So: ground AI recommendations in trusted sources — NN/g, MeasuringU, Baymard — and spot-check anything you'd be willing to act on.

That's the job that doesn't go away: judging whether the plausible thing is also the right thing.

try.q: What is the expertise AI can't supply?
options: Telling good output from plausible output
try.explain: Which is why the expert stays in the loop.

test.q: Why is bad UX a reason for optimism?
options: It shows how much work remains
It proves users tolerate poor design
test.explain: The basics are still being missed everywhere.

test.q: How old were the problems in the heuristic review?
options: They were new to the industry
test.explain: Hover-dependent navigation and mislabelled buttons are long-documented.

test.q: What is the caveat on the layoff figures?
options: Shares don't account for role population sizes
The data is from one country
Layoff directories exclude contractors and agencies
test.explain: UX may still be hit hard relative to its size.

test.q: How should AI recommendations be handled?
options: Grounded in trusted sources and spot-checked
Accepted whenever they match published best practice
